title: Compiler Architecture
snippet: How source code becomes a running program.

title: Pipeline overview
snippet: KelpyShark source code passes through four major stages before it is either interpreted or compiled to a target language: Lexer — text → tokens Parser — tokens → AST Semantic analysis — validate the A

title: 1. Lexer ( lexer.rs )
snippet: The lexer (scanner) reads raw source text character-by-character and produces a flat list of tokens . Each token has a kind (e.g. Ident , Number , String , Plus , If ) and a source location (line, col

title: 2. Parser ( parser.rs )
snippet: The recursive-descent parser consumes the token stream and builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) . Each node in the tree corresponds to a language construct (function definition, binary expression, if

title: 3. Semantic analysis ( semantic.rs )
snippet: After parsing, the semantic analyser walks the AST to catch errors that the grammar alone cannot detect: Use of variables before declaration return outside a function break / continue outside a loop D

title: 4. Code generation / interpretation
snippet: After semantic analysis, the validated AST can go to one of several backends: Backend Module Description Interpreter interpreter/ Tree-walking interpreter. Evaluates the AST directly. Used by kelpysha

title: Error handling
snippet: Errors are represented by the KSError type (defined in error.rs ). Each error carries a message and an optional source span (start line/col, end line/col) so the CLI can underline the offending code.

title: FAQ
snippet: Frequently asked questions about KelpyShark.

title: Do I need to install a separate runtime?
snippet: No. KelpyShark is distributed as a single self-contained binary. Download it, put it on your PATH, and you're ready to go. See the Setup page for instructions.

title: Is KelpyShark statically or dynamically typed?
snippet: Dynamically typed. Variables hold values of any type, and the type can change during the lifetime of the variable. Use type() to inspect the type at runtime if needed.

title: Do I need semicolons?
snippet: No. KelpyShark does not use semicolons as statement terminators. Just write each statement on its own line (or on consecutive lines — the language is whitespace-insensitive outside of string literals)

title: How do I read input from the user?
snippet: Use io.input(prompt) : import io let name = io.input("What is your name? ") print("Hello, {$name}!")

title: Can I use KelpyShark for web development?
snippet: You can build HTTP-based scripts (calling APIs, processing JSON, serving simple responses). A full web framework is not yet part of the standard library, but packages in the registry may provide one.

title: How do I share code between files?
snippet: Put shared code in a .ks file and use import : import utils # imports utils.ks from the same directory utils.my_function()

title: Why does type() return a string instead of a type object?
snippet: Simplicity. Returning a plain string means you can compare types with == without learning a separate type system. type(x) == "number" is immediately readable.

title: What happens if I divide by zero?
snippet: KelpyShark raises a runtime error: Division by zero . Catch it with try / catch if you need to handle that case.

title: Can I compile KelpyShark to Java or C#?
snippet: Yes. See the Code Generation page for details.

title: Where can I get help?
snippet: Open an issue on the GitHub repository, or check the Tutorial and Reference sections of these docs first.

title: Built-in Functions
snippet: Always-available functions — no import needed.

title: print(value)
snippet: Outputs value to the console followed by a newline. Example print("Hello") print(42) print(true) Output Hello 42 true

title: len(value)
snippet: Returns the length of a string or list. Example print(len("hello")) # 5 print(len([1, 2, 3])) # 3

title: type(value)
snippet: Returns a string describing the type of value . Example print(type(42)) # number print(type("hi")) # string print(type(true)) # boolean print(type(null)) # null print(type([])) # list print(type({}))

title: str(value)
snippet: Converts value to its string representation. Example let n = 3.14 let s = str(n) print(s + " is pi") # 3.14 is pi

title: num(value)
snippet: Converts a string to a number. Throws an error if the string is not a valid number. Example let x = num("42") print(x + 1) # 43 let y = num("3.14") print(y * 2) # 6.28

title: bool(value)
snippet: Converts a value to boolean. The following are falsy: false , null , 0 , "" , [] . Example print(bool(0)) # false print(bool(1)) # true print(bool("")) # false print(bool("hi")) # true print(bool([]))

title: range(stop) / range(start, stop) / range(start, stop, step)
snippet: Returns a list of numbers. Useful with for loops. Example print(range(5)) # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] print(range(2, 6)) # [2, 3, 4, 5] print(range(0, 10, 2)) # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] for i in range(3) { print(i) }

title: push(list, value)
snippet: Appends value to the end of list . Modifies the list in place. Example let nums = [1, 2] push(nums, 3) print(nums) # [1, 2, 3]

title: pop(list)
snippet: Removes and returns the last element of list . Example let items = ["a", "b", "c"] let last = pop(items) print(last) # c print(items) # ["a", "b"]
